issues.legal_issue: The filing period for a compensation-redetermination application based on another interested person’s court award runs from the date of that award, not from the applicant’s knowledge of it.
material_facts: Other interested persons whose land was covered by the same notification obtained an enhanced-compensation award on 3 April 2006.
The applicants had not sought a reference themselves. Their counsel applied for a certified copy on 17 May 2006; it was ready on 29 May and collected on 3 June.
The applicants filed their redetermination application on 18 July 2006. The Collector rejected it as four days late, and the applicants’ claimed date of acquiring knowledge was not substantiated.
issues.conclusion: The application period began from the date of the court’s award, with the day of the award and the time requisite for obtaining a copy excluded; the applicant’s date of knowledge did not affect the period. The dismissal of the application as late was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 28A(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires an application within three months from the date of the court’s award, excluding the day of the award and the time requisite for obtaining a copy. Under State of A.P. v. Marri Venkaiah, Union of India v. Mangatu Ram, Tota Ram v. State of U.P., Des Raj v. Union of India, and State of Orissa v. Chitrasen Bhoi, knowledge of the award is irrelevant to that period. Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. Deputy Land Acquisition Officer concerned Section 18 and does not govern Section 28A applications.

predicates.reassessment_request_based_on_another_in: A person who did not seek a reference requests reassessment based on a court award obtained by another interested person whose land was covered by the same acquisition notification.
predicates.statutory_period_measured_from_court_awa: The governing rule fixes the filing period by reference to the date of the court’s award and excludes the award day and the time requisite to obtain a copy.

issues.definition: When a person seeks reassessment based on another interested person’s court award and the filing period is fixed by reference to that award, the period runs from the award rather than from the applicant’s knowledge.

issues.legal_issue: The general limitation statute’s extension provisions do not apply to a compensation-redetermination application made to the Land Acquisition Collector under the statutory scheme.
material_facts: The application was made to the Land Acquisition Collector for redetermination based on a court award.
The Collector acts as a quasi-judicial authority, and the governing scheme specifies the period for making the application.
issues.conclusion: The Limitation Act, 1963, including its provision for extending time, did not apply; the application had to comply with the period prescribed by the governing land-acquisition provision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 prescribes the filing period for an application to the Collector. Union of India v. Mangatu Ram and Tota Ram v. State of U.P. hold that the Collector is not a court but a quasi-judicial authority and that the Limitation Act, 1963 does not apply to such an application.

predicates.application_is_made_to_quasi_judicial_co: A person makes the relevant application to an authority that acts in a quasi-judicial capacity rather than as a court.
predicates.governing_scheme_prescribes_filing_perio: The governing statutory scheme specifies a period within which the application must be made.

issues.definition: When an application is made to a quasi-judicial authority under a scheme that prescribes its filing period, the general limitation statute’s extension provisions do not apply.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot extend a statutory filing period on equitable grounds merely because applying it causes hardship or the legislation is beneficial.
material_facts: The applicants argued that the legislation was beneficial, that limitation should account for their knowledge of the award, and that the delay was minimal.
The application was held to be outside the period prescribed by the governing statute.
issues.conclusion: The statutory period had to be applied as written, and the court had no power to extend it on equitable grounds; the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The express filing period in Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 must be enforced according to its terms. A person seeking the benefit of the provision must act within the prescribed period. The Court relied on The Martin Burn Ltd. v. The Corporation of Calcutta and Rohitas Kumar v. Om Prakash Sharma for the principle that hardship or inconvenience does not authorize a court to disregard a statutory requirement.

predicates.application_is_subject_to_express_statut: The type of application is governed by a statute that expressly prescribes a filing deadline.
predicates.filing_is_outside_deadline: The application was filed after the deadline calculated under the governing statutory rule.

issues.definition: When an application is subject to an express statutory deadline and is filed after it, the court cannot extend that deadline on equitable grounds.
